nameStory: Staurastrum margaritaceum gets its genus name from the Greek words 'stauros' meaning cross and 'astron' meaning star, referring to its distinctive star-like shape with radiating arms. The species name 'margaritaceum' means 'pearly' in Latin, describing the beautiful pearl-like luster this tiny organism displays under microscopic light.
description: This is actually not a plant at all, but a microscopic single-celled algae that lives in freshwater ponds and lakes! Staurastrum margaritaceum is so tiny you'd need a microscope to see it - each cell is only about 30-50 micrometers across (smaller than the width of a human hair). It has a distinctive star or cross shape with symmetrical arms radiating outward, and appears bright green with a pearlescent sheen. These beautiful geometric organisms float freely in the water as part of the phytoplankton community.

idTips.label: Star-shaped symmetry
idTips.description: The cell has a distinctive cross or star shape when viewed from above, with arms radiating symmetrically from the center like a tiny green snowflake

idTips.label: Pearlescent shine
idTips.description: Under proper microscopic lighting, the cell wall displays a beautiful pearl-like luster that seems to shimmer and glow

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: The cell appears vibrant emerald green due to its chloroplasts, which are visible as darker green patches within the transparent cell wall

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Extremely small at 30-50 micrometers across - you'd need at least 400x magnification to clearly see the star-shaped structure

habitat: Found floating in clean, nutrient-rich freshwater ponds, small lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England's lower elevations. This species prefers slightly acidic to neutral water with good light penetration. Look for it in beaver ponds, kettle ponds, and the shallow margins of larger lakes where organic matter has accumulated.

seasonality.spring: Population begins to increase as water temperatures warm and daylight hours lengthen. Best collected from surface water samples in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when water temperatures are highest. Most easily found and identified during July and August sampling.
seasonality.fall: Numbers begin to decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases. Still present but less abundant in early fall pond samples.
seasonality.winter: Populations drop to very low levels or become dormant during winter months. Rarely observed in winter plankton samples from New England waters.

funFact: Despite being a single cell smaller than a speck of dust, Staurastrum margaritaceum can actually swim! It moves through the water using tiny whip-like flagella and can even respond to light by swimming toward or away from bright areas.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other star-shaped Staurastrum species, but the pearly luster and specific arm proportions help distinguish it. Remember: 'margarita' means pearl in Spanish - look for that characteristic pearlescent shine to confirm identification.
contextualKnowledge: Many people are surprised to learn that these organisms are classified as plants (in the broad sense) because they photosynthesize like trees and flowers, even though they're single-celled and live in water. They're part of a group called desmids, which are among the most geometrically beautiful organisms on Earth.
compareHints: Compared to other Staurastrum species in New England waters, margaritaceum is distinguished by its relatively smooth arms without prominent spines and its characteristic pearlescent cell wall. While Staurastrum aculeatum has spiny projections and Staurastrum hirsutum appears hairy, margaritaceum has a cleaner, more polished appearance that matches its 'pearly' name.
